rule: The center of interest is always in the light; the eye goes to light areas first.
Keep shadows thin, simple and transparent with little detail, so the eye passes over them to the next lit area.
Under a cool light source, shadows usually read best as warm colors, which look transparent and recede.
Place highlights where a plane changes direction or at the corners of forms.
In a light area let one element dominate - either value or color, not both; the brighter a highlight, the less color it shows.
Limit the number of distinct values (about three to five) and keep the value plan fixed once set.
The closer an object is, the more contrast, color, intensity and edge sharpness it has.
Dull or shift a color with its complement rather than with black or gray, which deadens it.
The color of the light source informs every lit area and unifies the image; shadows share its absence.
A single brushstroke should convey color or value, not both at once.
For hair-like masses such as thatch, paint the volume and pick out a few strands; the viewer extends the established pattern.
Cast shadows tend to warm up at their edges.
Massed shadow shapes need to be unified, not necessarily very dark, especially as they recede.
